question: Who was the British Governor-General during the Revolt of 1857?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Lord Canning**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Lord Canning** was the British Governor-General during the Revolt of 1857, also known as the First War of Indian Independence.
 
• He served as Governor-General of India from 1856 to 1858 and later as the first Viceroy of India from 1858 to 1862.
 
• Lord Canning introduced several reforms during his tenure, including the establishment of universities in Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras in 1857.
 
• After the revolt, the Government of India Act 1858 was passed, transferring power from the East India Company to the British Crown, marking the end of Company rule in India.
 
• Lord Canning is also known for his policy of conciliation, aimed at pacifying the Indians after the revolt by introducing measures like the Indian Councils Act of 1861.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Lord Dalhousie (1848–1856):**

 
 
• He was the Governor-General of India before Lord Canning and is known for his policy of annexation, called the Doctrine of Lapse.
 
• Important annexations during his tenure include Satara, Jhansi, Nagpur, and Awadh.
 
• He is credited with introducing railways, telegraphs, and postal systems in India, contributing significantly to modernizing the country.
 
 
 
• **Lord Curzon (1899–1905):**
 
 
• He is known for the controversial partition of Bengal in 1905, which led to widespread protests and ultimately the Swadeshi Movement.
 
• Lord Curzon also established the Archaeological Survey of India to protect and preserve India’s historical monuments.
 
 
 
• **Lord Ripon (1880–1884):**
 
 
• He is remembered for his liberal reforms, including the introduction of local self-government in India, making him popular among Indians.
 
• Lord Ripon also repealed the Vernacular Press Act of 1878 and introduced the Ilbert Bill, which sought to allow Indian judges to try British offenders.
